name: SNT and Consent: The Unconscious Patient Problem
author: GLMZ Emergency Medicine Ethics Committee
body:
When an unconscious patient arrives at an emergency department with life-threatening injuries, the standard of care may require cybernetic intervention — a replacement organ, a vascular bypass, a skeletal reinforcement to prevent spinal collapse. All of these require SNT bonding.

The patient cannot consent. They are unconscious, dying, or both. The physician must decide: bond chrome to this person’s body without their permission, or let them die.

The ethical framework is clear in theory: implied consent covers life-saving procedures. But SNT bonding is not like inserting a temporary breathing tube. It is permanent integration. The patient will wake up with a piece of technology that their brain will treat as part of their body. They will be dependent on SNT maintenance for as long as the implant remains. They will owe money for hardware they did not choose.

We have documented cases of patients who, upon regaining consciousness and learning they had been augmented without consent, experienced severe psychological distress. Some demanded immediate removal — a procedure that carries its own risks and leaves phantom chrome syndrome. Others accepted the augmentation but reported feelings of violation comparable to non-consensual body modification.

The most difficult cases involve the Unaltered Assembly and similar groups whose religious convictions prohibit augmentation. A physician who saves an Unaltered member’s life through SNT-bonded cybernetics has, in the patient’s view, committed a spiritual violation in the act of physical salvation. The body is alive. The patient considers it desecrated.

Current protocol: emergency SNT-bonded augmentation is authorized when no less-invasive option exists and death is imminent. The patient must be informed immediately upon regaining consciousness. Removal is offered if medically safe. Psychological support is mandatory. Financial obligation for the hardware is deferred pending patient decision.

This protocol satisfies no one. The physicians feel they are violating autonomy. The patients feel they were changed without permission. The corponations feel they are absorbing costs for hardware that patients may reject. The ethicists feel the protocol is a compromise that compromises everything.

But the alternative is letting people die because we are afraid to save them with the tools we have. So we bond the Saint to their flesh and hope they forgive us.
